newsitem.title: BELGIUM: Nigerian dissidents slam Dutch visa waiver plan.
newsitem.headline: Nigerian dissidents slam Dutch visa waiver plan.

text.p: Nigerian dissidents headed by exiled Nobel laureate Wole Soyinka condemned on Friday a Dutch plan to allow a Nigerian government minister to visit the Netherlands next month for an international conference.
Bolaji Akinyemi, foreign affairs spokesman for the Nigerian opposition group NADECO, said the invitation was a "flagrant violation of the EU's sanctions regime".
"It is not a helpful development at all. We are hoping that it is not too late for that invitation to be withdrawn," Akinyemi told a news conference.

The Dutch ran into political flak on Thursday for inviting Nigeria to attend a meeting in Maastricht of government leaders from the 15-member EU bloc and its partners from 70 African, Caribbean and Pacific (ACP) countries.
A foreign ministry spokesman for the Dutch, who hold the EU presidency, said on Thursday visa restrictions applied only to "Nigerian authorities travelling to Europe for private reasons".

Nigeria's government has been shunned by the United States and other Western governments since the 1995 hanging of writer Ken Saro Wiwa and eight other minority activists after a special court convicted them of murder.
The United States, the European Union and South Africa reacted later the same year by banning arms sales to Nigeria and imposing visa restrictions.

Soyinka criticised the actions as insufficient, urging the EU to take measures against Nigerian military leader General Sani Abacha, whose regime he said exceeded the worst cruelties of South Africa's apartheid era.
"What excuse can the international community have (for inaction)? Disinvest, apply the same measures that you took against South Africa," he told the same news conference.
He also questioned countries' motives for holding back, asking: "Is it because this time the oppressor is black?"
Earlier on Friday, the delegation met a senior Commission official in charge of relations with ACP countries.
Spokesman Joao Vale de Almeida said after the meeting the Commission had voiced "very clear support for a democratic and peaceful transition in Nigeria."
"The Commission will certainly keep up its pressure on General Abacha's regime," he told a news conference.

"The Commission will go on supporting human rights initiatives coming from the civil society in Nigeria. We do not associate the Nigerian regime with the Nigerian people, we make a clear distinction in that area," he said.
